utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Indah Susanti for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours may have seen - I hope that you were told from the e-mail I sent on Friday - in response to the Defence notification that they propose to add at that stage a further, I think it was 65, new documents, since yesterday 70 new documents to the list. Your Honours, between -- on their list, between tabs 210 and now 289 are, as I say, a further 79 documents that it is said that Mr. Zecevic proposes to use with this witness. Your Honour, can I saying straightaway, we have added about 49 documents this morning but the difference is that we have to add documents because the 65 ter summaries really do not tell you, nor indeed on this occasion did the interview we conducted with this witness, the sort of assertions he's going to be making. And so it's only as you listen to the evidence that you realise the documents that are going to become relevant. Whereas the Defence are presumed, as we were, when calling their witnesses in chief to have decided in advance through the lengthy proofing sessions they apparently conduct with their witnesses what documents they want to use. But, however, Your Honour, the documents, it's themselves that I want to raise. All of the documents relate to criminal cases in some form or another, either criminal complaints or forensic examination or the like. All of them relate to areas which are outside that of the CSB Sarajevo. And, therefore, this witness cannot possibly have any personal knowledge of these matters at all. The majority come from Banja Luka. There are 63 of the documents listed from the Banja Luka area, including municipalities, however, which are not covered by this indictment, but Your Honours have expressed the view before that leeway must be given. But they come from Laktasi, for example, Bosanska Gradiska on the Croatia border, Mrkonjic Grad, Glamoc and Celinac, Bosanska Dubica, and the like. Ten of the documents are related to Bijeljina. Your Honours have heard quite a lot of evidence about that they all relate to the murder of Krkic [phoen]. And seven relate to Doboj, all of which were dealt with by Mr. Bjelosevic when he gave evidence. Now, Your Honours, the Defence have decided, for whatever reason, not to call very many witnesses; that, of course, is their decision. But they can't, we would submit to you, try to deal with the consequences of that decision by making a witness, who patently cannot give evidence of his own knowledge, as it were, a vessel for producing documents that they have not otherwise been able to produce. A number of them, in fact, are MFI'd because Mr. Zecevic sought to put them in through Mr. Tutus, who one would have thought was clearly a witness who was at least closer to most of these criminal report and analyses. It turned out he couldn't say anything, Your Honours, and we objected on the basis that the -- that he was not the suitable witness for these documents to come in to. And this was left so that the documents that were shown to him were MFI'd. Your Honours, if Mr. Tutus wasn't suitable, then how can it be said that Mr. Tusevljak is even remotely suitable? Your Honours, the Defence could have called a witness who could deal with them. Of course Mr. Zupljanin, obviously, is in a position to deal with them. Or alternatively if they cannot find a witness then the proper way is to bar table them. But we would submit it's not proper to try and use this witness to get these documents into evidence. As I say, it escapes me at the moment entirely how he can give any useful or meaningful evidence about these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I'm sure Your Honours would recall the exchanges we had on the transcript of Friday, 20367. Your Honours, that is for the first time that the Defence was made aware of the Prosecutor's case. Namely, the Prosecution changed their case, and obviously even in -- during the Defence case they are modifying their case. First, in the indictment and the OTP pre-trial brief what was alleged was that our client participated in sham inquiries. Now, you will recall that during the Prosecutor's case we presented a number of documents which were criminal complaints filed. Then the Office of the Prosecutor changed their case again, stating that there was a discrimination in the way how the police worked and that in cases where the victims were Muslims or non-Serbs there was a completely different situation than in case where the victims were Serbs. Now, when we showed the documents, criminal complaints, which were filed in cases where the victims were non-Serbs, now we come to the point where Ms. Korner is suggesting that it is -- their case is not about whether the criminal complaints were filed in cases where non-Serbs were victims, but - and I'm quoting now: "We say there is no --"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page number is 22368, I believe, of Friday transcript. "But we say that there's no -- absolutely no evidence before the Court that any trials taking place 17 or 18 years later are based on the evidence recovered by the police in 1992. And that is a real issue." And then further: "That does not mean to say that any prosecution now is based on the evidence gathered or not gathered in 1992. And that's the issue." Now, confronted with that fact, which was stated for the first time, it became apparent to us for the first time during this last two years what is the Prosecutor's case. We decided to show the documents, which we have never proofed the witness with, but to show the documents to him concerning especially this allegation which Ms. Korner explicitly explained on Friday. Now, it is my understanding, Your Honours, that the guide-lines which require us to announce the documents is just that we put the parties on notice that we are going to use these documents, that we are going to use some of the documents for the -- during the direct examination of the witness, as well as cross-examination of the witness. Therefore, the moment when this became apparent to us what is the nature of the Prosecutor's case, I mean, the change in the Prosecutor's case, if I can say so, we informed all the parties that we are going to rely on -- that we are going to show some of these documents to the witness. That's the first part. The second part of Ms. Korner's words right now are actually misinterpretation of the situation which is in the case -- in this case. On page 7840 during the examination of Tusevljak -- the OTP Witness Tutus, I'm sorry. Your Honour Judge Hall: "Mr. Zecevic, if you are continuing to lead evidence from the witness to answer the second question that we posed, we are satisfied on that aspect. And now our ruling is that the documents may be marked for identification, not pending a further witness coming in to prove them, but pending the matter of authenticity being resolved at some point." Now, after that, Your Honours, if you will probably recall, the Defence informed the parties that the documents were received actually from the RS MUP, these documents which the authenticity is asked for, was questioned or objected by the Office of the Prosecutor, and we submitted the document which is now 65 ter 20187, and it's in Prosecutor's binder number 52. And that is the document where all these documents which were MFI'd are contained, and it's a confirmation by the RS MUP that these documents have been disclosed to us, and, therefore, we anticipated that this would have been sufficient to prove the authenticity of these documents. Now, as the matter was not resolved with that, this document which I just cited, the document 52 in the binder of the Office of the Prosecutor, was in fact signed by this witness, who is a co-ordinator of the team. And, therefore, what I intend to do with these documents is that I show this document to him to -- that he proves that this is his document and then I show him the example of these documents in order that he verifies the authenticity of the documents so we can ask that the documents be de-MFI'd. And that is the only reason, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that wasn't at all -- first of all, can I say, we have not changed our case. And for Mr. Zecevic to say he only heard this when we he had the discussion on Thursday cannot be right because apart from anything else we made that very self-same point in a written response to one of his motions for additions to the 65 ter list. But if all that he wants this witness to do is to have a list of the reports that are contained in his letter and say "Are those authentic?" then of course we don't object. What I do object to is for him going through all of these cases about which he has no personal knowledge whatsoever. He can simply say he received them and passed them on to the Defence. No objection to that at all. Whether Your Honours de-MFI it at that stage is a matter perhaps to see also when we hear from cross-examination. As I say, my only objection is to each and every one of these - how many documents did I say they were? - 70, I think, or whatever, being gone through with the witness who knows nothing about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So matter seems to have been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, yes. Do I understand that's all that Mr. Zecevic is going to do? So that we don't have to send the witness in and out of court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I said so. Your Honours, I have a brief matter to inform Your Honours about. Can we go into the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just wanted to put Your Honours on notice that it may be - and I appreciate that the Court's not very receptive to applications for leave to appeal - but it is of such -- we do consider this of such importance, given, as I say, I have to go and check which trial judgement it was, that we may well want to ask for leave to appeal if Your Honours are going to rule that all of them may be 92 bis, just so that Your Honours are on notice. This is not in terrorem but just that that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, if there are no other housekeeping matters, would the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, if the other plans about -- with regard to Mr. Macar wouldn't work, would a opening of your case in the next week be a possibility? In the next weeks, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand Your Honour. I'm afraid that's not possible. I was away from the courtroom several days precisely because I was trying to deal with these newly arisen problems. So at first I had this expert witness who was supposed to start the week of the 17th, starting the 17th. And that would have wrapped up our trial, at least as far as the part before the summer recess is concerned. I moved him forward by about seven days. He should have been in Belgrade on the 4th of July and then he would have been in The Hague on the 7th or the 8th. On the 11th we would have started his evidence and perhaps been able to complete that same day. So that was the idea. But I did have a contingency plan as well, to bring another witness, that's SZ-006. However, he underwent heart surgery in the meantime and I had to give him up. I probably won't be able to call that witness. Needless to say, we'll do everything within our power to make sure we have other witnesses lined up, but it's just not realistic to expect that we would be able to bring any witness at all over the next two weeks to start their evidence in this court. The most -- probably the expert witness Kolacevic [phoen] would be ready on the 11th. That's as much as I can say. Regardless of whether Mr. Macar is ready to testify that week, Witness Kolacevic has been moved forward -- moved backward by a full week, and he will be able to start on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So that witness would be able to start on the 11th and after he finishes you could have other witnesses? It's just to know whether we have a plan B in case Mr. Macar is not able to come on the 11th of July. And I suppose we have to make that decision some time before the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I said is as much as I can promise at this point in time, as much as I'm certain about. I'll do my best to bring other witnesses too, among those mentioned. Most of these witnesses don't have passports. That's one of the problems. Some of them are gainfully employed and find it difficult to get leave from their employers. One of these witnesses happens to be in Australia throughout this period, therefore the timing is quite inconvenient. We have a total of three witnesses who were scheduled to testify after the summer recess, yet are unable to make it. Nevertheless, we'll certainly do everything within our power. But I can't promise anything more to the Chamber at this point. I can't make any further commitments, and I can't promise any other witnesses before the summer recess with the exception of the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Another, but related, question: Will you make an opening statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. A short one, though. In my announcement I said that it would not exceed a single session, and we'll start with the evidence straightaway after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, good afternoon to you. Before Mr. Zecevic resumes his examination-in-chief, I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On Friday the 17th of June, at page 22388, I was showing you a document from Vlasenica invoking CSB Sarajevo document 0147892. The document is under seal and I won't be showing it to you now for that reason. Nevertheless, you said at that time that it might be useful to see what the document 01478/92 from Sarajevo CSB was about. That would have allowed you, as you claimed, to comment on the document that we were looking at at the time. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a look at 1D584. This is tab 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Zecevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, is this the document that you said you would need to look at in order to see what was being requested?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. There are references here to our own documents, 123/92, the 25th of July, 1992. And you can also see that the public security stations were familiar through this document with the order of the minister of the interior, saying that all policemen should be removed from police stations who have criminal records of any kind or have been known to commit crimes during their work with the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document in front of you, does it have anything to do with the rules on disciplinary measures, war time disciplinary measures, and the violations of the terms of service, those more serious as well as those less serious, as described in the rules?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please move on to 194. 949D1. Tab 194. The document is 65 ter 949D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, was the public security station part of the Sarajevo Romanija-Birac district during 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is one of their documents, the 24th of September, 1992. The subject reads "response to your document 478/92," signed by Vujadin Klisaric. Are you familiar with this person, Mr. Klisaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, he was the chief of the Sekovici Public Security Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They report here that disciplinary proceedings were underway against one employee. It reads: "The proposal has already been submitted to the CSB for their information and for them to take steps." Do you perhaps remember what this was about?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember at the moment what specific employee this was about, but you can tell that steps have been taken against one of their own and the whole case file was forwarded to the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I've said over and over again that we don't say and we never have said that disciplinary proceedings were not carried out. The question is whether they were carried out for crimes committed against non-Serbs. And we don't even know what this one's for. But other than that, Your Honours, if Your Honours want to admit it, we don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: How does this advance the case, Mr. Zecevic, the admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I explained already once and the document I referred to at that time was admitted. It is important for the Defence because it reflects the knowledge of the minister, the ministry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah, but if I might interrupt, as Ms. Korner says, on the face of it, we don't know what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's about the disciplinary proceedings conducted against one of the members of the MUP. It says in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: For what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the point is not for what, with all due respect. The point is that the disciplinary system exists at the time, and that is the knowledge of the accused. Your Honours -- Your Honours, please, the law lists what are the major -- or the important or less important breaks of the duties of the police officers. The law of the Ministry of Interior, the Law on Public Administration. We established that the -- that there was an instruction on the disciplinary proceedings -- Perhaps the witness can take the headphones off. We established that there was an instruction signed by minister on the disciplinary proceedings during the state of war. Now, if the minister in 1992 is aware that the disciplinary system functions, that the disciplinary -- that the disciplinary measures were taken against the members of the MUP, I think that goes to the knowledge and therefore is very relevant for our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the document may be -- is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D592, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Tusevljak. Can we now please have 65 ter 142D1. This is tab 59. Rather, can we please first have 943D1 from tab 917. My apologies. 934. 934D1, tab 197.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a dispatch from the public security station in Zvornik, sent to the Ministry of the Interior, police administration, Security Services Centre in Bijeljina, as well as that in Sarajevo, the Romanija-Birac CSB, signed by Chief Milorad Lokancevic. This document reports on a disciplinary procedure that is being initiated against a person called Brano Djurdje, son of Milan, the police employee. In the last paragraph, the chief suggests that this person be suspended from work because of a serious violation. Sir, are you familiar with Mr. Milorad Lokancevic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the chief of the Zvornik Public Security Station at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you look at the type of violation committed by this member of the public security station, is this what you might classify as a serious violation of his obligations?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The proper question is: "How would you classify this?"

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Madam Korner is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How would you classify this work-related violation based on the description in the document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite obvious that the document states that the police employee committed a violation. He caused an instance of public danger and he was found to be in possession of a substantial amount of weapons. Therefore, this constitutes a serious violation of work discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about the actions taken by this member of the MUP, do they have any features that would constitute a crime or a criminal offence, and if so, which?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're looking at the criminal offence of causing public danger and possession of illegal weapons and ammunition. I can't specifically remember the articles in the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina that relate to these criminal offences, but there appears to be a total of two criminal offences involved here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a member of -- or, rather, what about members of the Ministry of the Interior who committed violations such as this one or even more serious ones, were they suspended, and if so, at what point in time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were suspended. The measure would be taken as soon as the circumstances were explained under which a criminal offence had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the same reason as that which was raised in relation to the previous document, I would like to tender this one into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D593, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have 65 ter 142D1, tab 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the date on this document is the 22nd of September, 1992, Zvornik Public Security Station, signed by Milorad Lokancevic. Reference is to a dispatch by the Sarajevo Security Services Centre, which is also the addressee. There is a reference to this dispatch that unfortunately is not in our possession, dispatch number 477. On the 20th of August, a criminal report was filed because of a criminal offence from Article 43 of the Criminal Code of the SRJ, war crimes against the wounded and sick. It also says that a questionnaire was filled out, war crimes victims questionnaire, and attached to this memo. First of all, did you receive from the Ministry of Interior at any point in May 1992 a set of instructions or guide-lines on what to do in case you came across any war crimes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, it was in the latter half of May. A letter came that said we should take steps if we came across any of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember who signed that letter, that communication?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was signed by the then chief of the crime police administration, Dobro Kanjic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you perhaps remember that at any point throughout the summer of 1992 -- or, rather, during the summer of 1992 did you receive any other guide-lines that had to do with war crimes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had this collegium meeting at the Ministry of Interior in Belgrade. One of the conclusions reached was that appropriate measures had to be taken to document war crimes. I'm not sure if there was a special dispatch that was sent out to everyone dealing with war crimes, but I know that at some point late that summer forms were distributed to everyone that were to be filled by everyone at public security stations across the range that had to do with war crimes. I think that we from the Security Services Centres at some point in August or possibly in September drew up some framework guide-lines on what to do whenever one came across the commission of a war crime in the line of duty. We had a very experienced criminal technician who worked with us and he produced a sort of mock scenario as to what a technician like that, a forensic officer, should do when they came across a crime scene. It's related to what I was saying before. When on the ground, unfortunately we didn't have sufficiently-trained employees who were trained in a way that would have allowed them to deal with this type of crime. Regrettably they weren't even sufficiently trained to deal with ordinary crimes. For the most part, they had no experience with the more serious crimes. So the report that reached the Security Services Centre is precisely in relation to the intensions that arose in the latter half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one intervention in the transcript. On page 21, line 10: "Regrettably they weren't even sufficiently trained to deal with ordinary crimes." I think you said something else. Can you please slowly repeat your answer so that it would be correctly recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in this part of my answer that they were not trained to conduct investigation of the most ordinary criminal offences, such as theft, aggravated theft. That is to say, the classic crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the reason for you to draw up these instructions for the forensic technicians during the month of August 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we saw that documents which we were receiving from the ground, from police stations, did not meet the most basic needs. And it is well known that what forensic technicians collect at the sites of crimes is then submitted to the prosecutor's offices so that the prosecutor's office could present the evidence before a court. Which means that the on-site investigations which were conducted by the forensic technicians were not nearly adequate. That was the reason to assist, at least a little, the forensic technicians who had begun working on the ground. In the Ministry of the Interior no forensic -- no courses for forensic technicians had been organised as yet at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was the goal to improve the work of the forensic technical service or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only improving the work of the forensic technicians on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let us return to the document. Are you familiar with the first item, a criminal report? What does it have to do with?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot specifically say judging by the numbers and the date which criminal offence this was, but it is obvious that the Zvornik Public Security Station submitted this against unknown perpetrators with the basic public prosecutor's office in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, this document talks about a report dated the 26th of June, 1992, when genocide was committed against the Serbian population in the territory of the Serbian population in Zvornik. And the reasons for which criminal reports against unidentified persons or, as they are called here, the Muslim extremists had not been submitted. Tell me, Mr. Tusevljak, did the police have a different standard when it came to war crimes committed against non-Serbs as compared to those instances when the victims were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When the police went out to a crime site and conducted an on-site investigation, when we were called and when we could conduct an on-site investigation, the same criminal report against unidentified person was filed if the perpetrators were unidentified. And if the perpetrators of a crime were known, then most often, when such persons were within our reach, criminal reports were filed for crimes of aggravated murder. Article 36, I think, paragraph 3 or 4, but I cannot say that off the top of my head, but these were -- this was the most serious crime. And this paragraph in the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina envisaged the most severe penalties as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will show you these documents awhile later. Now, please tell me, do you remember whether there were any requests to document war crimes, particularly, or crimes against civilians committed against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all requests asked for all war crimes to be documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Why was it sometimes insisted that crimes against Serbs documented as well?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were always committed in 90 per cent of the cases at least. Territory which was not under the control of the Republika Srpska MUP. Therefore we mostly learned of them through Serbs who had managed to survive the crimes. It happened very often that we could not reach these persons because they wouldn't report to any police station, so that very often we only learned about those crimes quite some time after they had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Once again for the needs of the transcript, page 23, line 21, to my question "was it sometimes insisted that crimes against Serbs be documented as well," your answer has been recorded in the following way: "Because they were always --" the crimes were in at least 90 per cent of the cases committed, and then full stop. "The territory which was under the control of the Republika Srpska MUP. Therefore we mostly learned of them through Serbs who had managed to survive the crimes." This is not what you said. It is very important, so can you please explain for us what this is about, which crimes this refers to, and please be so kind and say it in a slow and articulate manner so that it would be recorded precisely.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crimes against Serbs were committed in 90 per cent of the cases in the territory which was under the control of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the MUP of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina rather than in the territory which was under the control of the Republika Srpska MUP. That was the reason why our ability of learning that a crime had been committed was limited to Serbs who had come as refugees from these areas. Very often these refugees did not report themselves to any police station and did not report these events. For that reason, it was requested that operatives interview such persons and take their statements so that through such statements such crimes would be documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's provide a context for this or an example so that we could understand it better. If you learned that a crime had been committed against some Serbs who were in the territory of Sarajevo controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would that constitute such a case?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the only way at the time in which we could receive such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And as for the Ministry of the Interior of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was under the control of the Ministry of the Interior, did it submit criminal reports in case of such crimes or document them, from what you know, if you know anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] How can he answer that question? He's not a member of the MUP of BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I asked if he's aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I still ask: How can he answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the witness can answer --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. You explain to me on what basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the witness's testimony is that ministry of RS is filing criminal complaints against the perpetrators of crimes committed against the Serbs in the territory which was not under their control, and I'm asking him whether he knows if the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina filed the criminal complaints for these very same crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I appreciate and -- I appreciate that is the question. I'm sorry, Your Honours, we should do it through you. I appreciate that's the question. I'm merely querying the basis on which a member of the MUP of the RS can know whether or not the MUP in BiH, across the front lines which he's described so vividly, so often, can know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he explained that they were getting this information from the people who managed to escape from the territory which was under the control of the Bosnian army, so perhaps he has -- he has knowledge through that. And it is admissible in this jurisdiction, I believe. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you have information of this kind?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we absolutely did. I'm still investigating war crimes, and I have had opportunity to see all criminal reports filed since 1992 in Bosnia and Herzegovina to this very day. I'm currently co-operating with prosecutors at the cantonal prosecutor's office in Sarajevo and I have access to all files submitted by the Sarajevo Police between 1992 and 1995, and after that. I also have access to everything that was submitted to the military cantonal prosecutor's office in Sarajevo. I have not come across a single criminal report from that time which has to do with war crimes except for criminal reports filed against Serbs and Croats. However, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I think this is also the case in other countries, the prosecutor is the person who determines how a certain act is to be qualified regardless of what we from the police may write and how we may classify an offence. That was the reason why the prosecutor sometimes changed the qualification of many criminal offences, both of those submitted by the police of the Federation and those submitted by the minister [as interpreted] of the interior of Republika Srpska. That is the absolute right of the prosecutor, to judge by the characteristics of a certain offence and change the qualification. What is most important in police work is that the report should contain as many elements as possible and as much evidence as possible about the act itself which was committed or evidence about the person who committed the act. I think I made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just another intervention in transcript. On page 27, line 3, you said criminal reports submitted by the police of the Federation or those submitted by the "minister" of the interior of Republika Srpska. Did you say "minister" or the "ministry"?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if a serious crime is committed in the territory that was outside Republika Srpska, whose duty was it to file a criminal report in accordance with the law, that is to say, who was supposed to prosecute the crime?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the Criminal Code or the Law on Criminal Procedure which was in force, the report should be submitted by the local police. However, it was standard that such reports about information that crimes had been committed were filed both by the MUP of Republika Srpska to its own prosecutor's office, and, as far as I know, our colleagues from the Federation, if they learned that some crimes had been committed in the territory of Republika Srpska, they also submitted such reports to their prosecutor's office. I think that there was a term on both sides at the time, of temporarily occupied territory, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, if you're going on to something else, perhaps we could take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in, and he can be brought in, can I just ask, in respect to Mr. Krgovic's 92 bis witnesses, and Your Honours said that you were minded to grant it, does that mean, in other words, that they wouldn't attend for cross-examination under 92 bis (c)?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That remains open.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That remains open. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That remains open.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, another clarification. At page 27/22, you said it was usual for such reports or information on crimes committed to be submitted by the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, to their own prosecutors, and, as far as I know, to the colleagues from the Federation. If the colleagues from the Federation learned of any crimes committed in the territory of Republika Srpska, they would submit these reports to their own prosecutor. When you say the "ministry," who exactly do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the organisational units of the Ministry of the Interior, the Security Services Centres or public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In cases like that, when you had information regarding a crime that was committed under the -- under the -- on territory that was under the control of the opposite side, would you file criminal reports in cases like that? And what supporting material would you normally attach to such a criminal report?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Criminal reports would be filed with the relevant prosecutor. Normally one would attach such evidence as was available at the time of the filing. Normally statements, no more than statements, taken from any witnesses or survivors. Whenever there were medical documents available concerning any injuries that had occurred, those files would be submitted too, along with the rest of it. If bodies were exchanged and if we were invited by the military security people to give them a hand, because, as you will realise, it was the military prosecutor that was in charge of these matters at the time, and the reports would go to the military prosecutor. So whenever that was the case, we would give a hand to our colleagues from the military security to examine the bodies forensically. Or if there was a pathologist who was available to conduct a postmortem, we would give the pathologist a hand with that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, would the hypothetical perpetrators of these crimes, or the presumed perpetrators, be within reach of the organs of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When I said hypothetical, I meant alleged perpetrators. Not hypothetical perpetrators. Based on what you know when criminal reports like these were made in relation to crimes against Serbian people in territory that was not under the control of the organs of Republika Srpska, would the relevant prosecutors then take up these cases?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part the prosecutors did not take any steps when such reports were received. You can tell that that was the case because up to this very day not even one per cent of those crimes have been dealt with successfully, and it has been 19 years since.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document, 65 ter 142D1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D594, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you perhaps remember this: What about crimes encompassed by the Federal Criminal Law of the former SFRY, crimes against humanity international law, such as genocide, war crimes against civilian population, against prisoners of war, and so on and so forth, do you remember what maximum penalty was envisaged for crimes like that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The maximum penalty envisaged for crimes like that was up to 15 years' imprisonment or death penalty, which could have been exchanged for a 20-year prison sentence. Nevertheless, as far as I know, sometime around 1990 or 1991 the federal Assembly abolished the dealt penalty and it was no longer part of the state law, so the only thing that remained was the maximum prison sentence of 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say abolished and was no longer part of the state law, which state law do you have in mind, or which legislation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These crimes were defined by the federal law, the Federal Criminal Code of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, chapter 15, I believe. These crimes, as such, did not exist in the republican criminal codes, and those were the ones that we had been using for our work in Bosnia and Herzegovina up until 1992. In about 90 per cent of the cases that we dealt with - when I say "we," I mean those of us dealing with the more general crimes - we used the Criminal Code of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to guide us in our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the Chamber's reference, Criminal Code of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia is part of the case file in this case, L11, chapter 16, Articles 141 through 149.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, what about the crime of murder, was that a matter for the federal law or was that a matter for the republican legislations?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The republican ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, what about the crime of qualified murder which at the time -- or, rather, let me ask you this first: What about the provisions of the criminal legislation of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did those apply throughout the territory of Republika Srpska in 1992 as well?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a law that was simply copied and remained the same as the one back in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Again it wasn't recorded. You said that "it was copied and remained the same as the one ... in 1992." Did you say that or did you say something else, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until 1992, that's what I said. The same laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, what about the laws that applied in Republika Srpska, what punishment was envisaged for the crime of qualified murder under that law?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The maximum prison term, 15 years, or a sentence of up to 20 years or the dealt penalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I didn't understand whether this was the situation from 1992 and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let us try and clarify this. Did the Republika Srpska adopt its own criminal code, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Republika Srpska adopted its own criminal code. I can't remember at which Assembly meeting. Nevertheless, the criminal code that was adopted by Republika Srpska was no more than a copy of the same law from the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were no changes. Not a single article was changed, not a single chapter was changed. Therefore, a crime of murder, Article 36, was handled the same way in the criminal code that applied in Bosnia-Herzegovina up to 1992 as well as in the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does this clarify the matter, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes and no, because I thought that the witness told us that the dealt penalty was abolished --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And so if the dealt penalty was abolished before the creation of the Republika Srpska, then how come that in the RS Penal Code certainly the death penalty reappeared? That was the thing that I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about two laws here. The Law of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia Criminal Code defining war crimes as a crime. The federal Assembly abolished the death penalty for that crime. The Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in which the crime of murder was included, no decision was taken to abolished death penalty. Therefore, the republican criminal code still had the crime of murder which still drew a dealt penalty, potentially, both prior to 1992 and at the beginning of 1992. I think sometime during the war the Assembly of Republika Srpska introduced an amendment to that. But one should go back to the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska, go through the old copies, to see whether a moratorium was in fact imposed on the execution of the death penalty. So we are looking here at two different laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you say "during the war," which period do you have in mind specifically, during 1992 or after 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From where I stand now, it's difficult for me to say. I really can't say. I just know that the decision was taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm reluctant to interrupt because it normally wastes more time, but surely all of this can be the subject of an admission if necessary, or we've got all the laws in the law library. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's on. I'm not at all clear why this witness, who is not a lawyer in any event, is being taken through it. It does seem to be an awful waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It will be clear, Your Honours, once I come to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, bearing this in mind, was the more severe punishment envisaged for the crime of qualified murder than that imposed in the case of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the amendment that was made, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And when the amendment was made, what was the relation between the war crimes on the one hand and the qualified murder on the other, in terms of the punishment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same punishment was envisaged for both crimes, and the range was the same, 10, 15, or even 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a note for the transcript, Your Honours, I see it was -- it's been translated "qualified murder" as it stands, qualified murder. It's aggravated murder, actually. When I say, in Serbian, [B/C/S spoken], means aggravated murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We figured as much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I -- you know, again it's probably the interpreters, but I think we need the interpreters to confirm that's it, not what Mr. Zecevic says he says it means.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are happy to confirm that Mr. Zecevic is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... can we call the transcript -- the interpreters to confirm? Thank you very much. Much appreciated. Your Honours, for the reference of the Trial Chamber, the document is in our law library, however -- the Criminal Code, I mean, is in the law library, republican Criminal Code, and, however, it has the P number, P119, and what we were discussing was the Article 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, in your capacity as head of the service for combatting crime in the Sarajevo Birac-Romanija centre, in situations where you were dealing with the crime of murder where the perpetrators and victims belong to different ethnic groups, back in 1992 how would the police qualify these crimes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crime of murder, well, Article 36, paragraph 4, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did this apply to situations in which the perpetrator of the crime was an ethnic Serb and the victims belonged to other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As for the crimes committed in our territory, regardless of the ethnicity of the perpetrator or the victim, depending on the actual crime, more often than not this was aggravated murder, we would file for murder, Article 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your answer to my first question was "no," but from the contents of your answer it seems to me that something else would follow. So can I rephrase the question because maybe I did not make myself clear. If a murder was committed in which a Serb was the perpetrator, or the supposed perpetrator, and the victims were of other ethnicity, how was such a criminal offence qualified during the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the crime of murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If the opposite was the case, namely, if the perpetrator of the crime was of a different ethnicity and the victim was a Serb, how was that qualified during the year 1992 as far as you know as the then chief of the Sarajevo CSB?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was in our territory, it was also treated as the crime of murder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That was translated as he was the chief of the CSB, which he wasn't as far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shortened it, so it's my mistake. What I had in mind was chief of the crime prevention administration at the Sarajevo CSB. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell me this, a practical question: When you filed these criminal reports against believed perpetrators who were of other ethnicity, did the prosecutor's offices, as far as you know, treat such criminal reports differently than instances in which the perpetrators were Serbs, perpetrators of the same crimes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as I know, the prosecutor's offices treated equally all reports submitted by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, once you file a criminal report, as there is suspicion that a criminal offence has been committed, for example, the crime under Article 36, paragraph 4, aggravated murder, is the prosecutor's office bound by your criminal report in the sense of the qualification of a crime?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The prosecutor has complete freedom, and the prosecutor is the one who determines the qualification of the crime. That is to say, he can change it, say that it is not that particular crime but, rather, a different one. And our further obligation, in case the prosecutor judges that the police or the minister [as interpreted] of the interior can submit new evidence or conduct certain checks, then he would address us with a request to collect previous information. And in accordance with such a request, we would then do what we had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Once again it says here that our obligation, in case the prosecutor -- if you received such a request from the prosecutor or a court, that the police or the minister of the interior can submit new evidence or conduct certain checks. Once again, did you say the "minister" or did you say the "ministry"?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say the minister, but I said that when we talk about the ministry we talk about members of the crime police or police. The prosecutor addresses the local police station directly. He does not even address the Security Services Centre. That was very often the case. The basic prosecutor's offices, the district prosecutor's offices, or the military prosecutor's offices had their territorial or actual jurisdiction. On the basis of this jurisdiction, whether it's territorial or actual, they would address their orders directly to police stations on the ground. And they did not have any obligation to inform the Ministry of the Interior about that. We have to make a distinction here between three levels in the MUP of Republika Srpska. In the first level is the ministry and its services at the ministry's seat. The second level are the Security Services Centres and their services at the centre's seat. And the third level are the public security stations and their services. The prosecutor's offices are almost always in co-ordination only with the lowest-level police stations. And if the services of the Security Services Centre submitted criminal reports, then they would communicate with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, just to clarify a terminological problem, when you say "territorial" or "local," are these two synonyms in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know that on 37 and somewhere before it was translated as "territorial or actual," where it means practically the same thing in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I will show you a document, 378D1. It is tab 128. Sir, this is a document from the basic public prosecutor's office in Zvornik. The date is the 26th of May, 1993, submitted to the lower court and the investigating judge in Zvornik. And it says: "Please find enclosed a criminal report of the Bratunac Public Security Station of" a certain number "dated the 25th of May, 1992, against Zoran Tomasevic." And then later on the request says that there are reasonable grounds to suspect that at around 1430 hours on the 20th of May, 1992, that person committed a criminal offence against the underaged Meva Husic by which he committed the crime of attempted rape pursuant to Article 88, and this is signed by deputy public prosecutor. Sir, is this a document or, rather, a request to open investigation? What kind of a document is that in the procedural sense?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we submit a criminal report to a prosecutor's office - when I say "we," I mean the police - according to the Law on Criminal Procedure which was then in force in Republika Srpska, the prosecutor when he assesses that there is sufficient evidence, then he submits precisely such a request to the investigating judge. And it is now up to the investigating judge to use the evidence submitted by the prosecutor as the basis on which he makes a decision. If there is sufficient evidence, the investigating judge makes a decision to conduct an investigation. And if the evidence is insufficient, he then makes a decision that an investigation would not be conducted and he sends it back to the prosecutor. So this is the standard legal procedure which was in force in Republika Srpska at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, once the investigating judge establishes that there are not enough elements to open an investigation and sends back a case to the prosecutor, does he give an order to that effect to the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The prosecutor can collect new evidence if he has it and resubmit them to the investigating judge. I think that there was the possibility of legal remedy as well, that is to say, the prosecutor could send a request to a trial chamber so that it would make a decision if the prosecutor did not agree with the decision to not open an investigation. And I think that the decision of the trial chamber was final.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, can you tell us on the basis of the first and last name in this request to open an investigation what was the ethnicity of the damaged party?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is evident that it is a person of Bosnian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the person reported as the perpetrator, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you perhaps familiar with this case, as this is the Bratunac Public Security Station which was in your territory, the territory of your Security Services Centre, that is to say?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report which was submitted as early as in 1992 was certainly something we were informed about regularly at the end of the year. This case should have been included in the report of the Public Security Station Bratunac when it informed us about the number of criminal reports submitted, who they were submitted to, and against whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D595, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the witness 906D1. Tab 203.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this while you are still looking for that document: Do you know whether in Bosnia-Herzegovina or Republika Srpska today there are any prosecutions based on criminal offences committed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll stipulate to that. There are indeed many cases going on at the state court in particular which relate to 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As Ms. Korner made things easier for us, for which I'm grateful to her, tell me whether you know whether the documents which the organisational units of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska drew up during 1992 with reference to particular crimes are being used in the criminal proceedings which are currently ongoing before these courts?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the job I'm doing at the moment. I work with the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina and with other prosecutors' offices in Bosnia and Herzegovina on specific cases. I know which documents are available to us in these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, the documents from 1992 which exist, what is the weight that they have?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all cases where there are reports on on-site investigations that were conducted then, photo files, expert reports, certificates on entry into apartments, receipts for items seized, various expert analyses which were carried out at the forensic centre in Banja Luka, which was founded in 1992, are irrefutable evidence and they are accepted by the trial chamber. In cases when statements weren't taken and were not taken, in accordance with the current Law on Criminal Procedure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the prosecutor's office is obliged or perhaps it may invest such an authority to the organs of the Ministry of the Interior to take a statement from the same person again but in accordance with the new legal regulations. Only if the person deceased in the meantime, then the prosecutor or the defence may offer such a statement as a piece of evidence during the trial. But then most often the authorised official who took such a statement is also called so that such a document could serve as evidence before a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The document in front of you is a judgement from the district court in Banja Luka from 2007 against Goran Petic, Zoran Djukic, Mladen Djukic, and Goran Djukic. As we can see on pages 3 and 4, it is for the criminal offence of war crime against civilians. On page 4 of the Serbian version, we can see the sentence. Are you familiar with this case?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This case was something that the department for war crimes of the Banja Luka Security Services Centre dealt with. It was the crime police sector, together with the prosecutor in charge. Inter alia, I co-ordinate the work of this department.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. No, I think, Your Honours, I'm now coming to an objection. The only connection that I understand that this witness has with this document for Banja Luka is his job as what he calls co-ordinating war crimes. He doesn't know anything other than what he sees himself, which we can all read. As I said, if the whole point is simply to get the document into evidence and this is a document that he supplied the Defence with, that's one matter. But the actual contents of all of this, Your Honour, I object to. I do say he's not a witness who can speak to this simply by reading what we can all read.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether in this case documents obtained in 1992 have been used?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these documents are from 1992. Can I just explain. The prosecutor's office is in Republika Srpska. With the passing of a new law, whenever there were cases of crimes when we accused someone for the crime of murder, this was pre-qualified into the crime of war crime on the basis of orders which we receive, and this is just one judgement. Since 2006 to this day only in Banja Luka, the court sentenced various Serbs to 247 years in prison for having committed war crimes. In all these sentences, the court referred to evidence which the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska submitted in 1992 inter alia. This is my current job, therefore, I could talk about all other prosecutor's offices in Republika Srpska. I could say how many investigations have been opened precisely about such crimes and on the basis of reports filed by the Republika Srpska MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify another terminological imprecision, on page 43 in line 9, you said that they were changed or pre-qualified from a crime of murder into the crime of war crime. Can you tell us: This term which was used here is pre-qualified, literally, but what does that mean when something is pre-qualified by a prosecutor? Can you just explain that for us?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a prosecutor receives a report from the Ministry of the Interior or any of its organisation units, has the discretion to look at the features of the crime and reclassify that crime, as it were, if that is what he sees fit to do. We are not necessarily dealing with a murder or a war crime. Someone, for example, is suspected of having committed grievous bodily harm and the prosecutor defines it or has it reclassified as less serious bodily harm or slight bodily harm, aggravated theft -- or theft reclassified as aggravated theft, and so on and so forth. There are numerous examples where you see a prosecutor receive a police report and subsequently reclassifying or redefining the crimes contained therein. This is a matter of daily practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've heard this evidence about five times from five different witnesses and we accept it, that the prosecutor has the right to reclassify an offence, whatever the police put in it. Your Honours, we've gone on without my objection being ruled on. My objection remains the same because unless this witness is going to tell us that he's read through every word of the file, attended the trial, and knows exactly what was led, then simply all he can say is this was based on a criminal report filed in, whenever it was, 1992. But he cannot say anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the only reason I returned the witness was that it was recorded as "pre-qualified" and I wanted to clarify that, that is, for the benefit of the transcript. Because in my understanding pre-qualified doesn't mean much in a legal sense in English. Now, the second thing, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have the witness take his earphones off, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the standard which Ms. Korner now is imposing is a quite different one from throughout the Office of the Prosecutor's case, when they presented their evidence. However, the only point that interests me in this -- in respect to all these judgements that I have listed, from 203, 284, tab 286, -87, -88, and -89, is precisely to show that the documentation gathered in 1992 is used in fact to bring the perpetrators in justice in 2006, 2007, 2008, 2009, or even today. And that was the gist of Ms. Korner's comment on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, you misunderstood. Let me make this absolutely clear. As I said at the time, no doubt at all that where trials have followed 18 years later, they may have been based on the original criminal reports filed. What we're saying is there's nothing to suggest in any of these documents that when the trials are finally held, as here in 2007 or thereabouts, that it is the evidence gathered in 1992 - which is obviously part of it, I agree, if there were forensic examination - which results in the conviction. That's what our contention is. Not that it wasn't used in the sense that Mr. Zecevic is now saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So perhaps then I need to go through the judgement to show that that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You wouldn't know the entire file, would you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, but, Your Honours, it's -- our judgements are listed because the requirement by the law is that the court explains or lists the evidence on which it based it judgement or all evidence presented during the case they were sitting on or deciding upon. And if we look at these -- all these documents, all these judgements, it is very clear that in all of them there is a lot of evidence gathered in 1992, which is precisely the point which Ms. Korner is making, which is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a minute. Let me just put the question, then: Is it your contention, Mr. Zecevic, that the judgements in 2002, 2003, 2004, 2005, 2006, and 2007 and so on were based exclusively on the evidence collected in 1992? Or might there have been other evidence coming in, in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course there is -- there was new evidence. Even in this trial there has been 50-odd number of new witnesses after the Office of the Prosecutor filed their indictment. Of course there is new evidence. But the point is, Your Honours: If there is a single document, a single statement, taken in 1992, that is sufficient for our purposes because that shows that the Ministry of the Interior was -- actually conducted as much as they can under these circumstances in 1992 their investigations. Filed a criminal report with the attachments, whatever the attachments are. They might not be as good as it is required, but the point of the matter is that they exist, and based on them, not exclusively on them, but based on them, in some cases exclusively, the judgements are taken 18 years after. That is a point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, Your Honours, this is impossible of resolution, quite honestly. We go down such a side track as to with us -- them calling evidence of these files or us calling -- recalling the evidence that was called in these trials that led to these judgements. Your Honours, if it assists, we're not saying that no criminal reports were filed. We are not saying that no statements were taken. We say what Mr. Zecevic has just said is a matter for argument at the end of the day and not susceptible to what he's trying to do with this witness. It is -- if Your Honours looked at this thing, it would be almost impossible to tell when the particular statements that they obviously relied on were taken. But, Your Honours, this is such a side track from the main issues of the trial that we say it is open to Mr. Zecevic to enter into evidence through a bar table motion such of these criminal cases as he wishes to and for us then to respond. It is not the way to take it through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I find myself entirely in agreement with Ms. Korner about this being a collateral issue which doesn't assist us at all, or if so, only marginally. So why are we spending so much time on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, because that's the Prosecutor's case, and I'm trying to rebut the Prosecutor's case. And I have the document here, I have the judgements where they list the documents from 1992. And the Prosecutor says these documents are not there, and I'm saying, yes, they are. And I'm showing the documents, the judgements, where I claim all these documentation, and the forensic reports and the other expert reports are contained.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Made in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, that's fine. Mr. Zecevic is perfectly entitled to submit these through a bar table motion. What he's not entitled to do is to take this witness through it. It -- he is not a witness who can do anything more than read what anybody else can read.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, but I don't see how is that different from all the Prosecutor expert witnesses, because they read through all the documents and actually testified about what they read about in the documents. With all due respect, this witness is involved in the -- in the war crimes as a co-ordinator of Republika Srpska concerning the war crimes, investigation of war crimes, and is very well aware of each and every of these cases and judgements. And he can provide the firsthand evidence about the contents of these files.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He can say "I've read the files." That's the absolute limit of what he can say. And my understanding was, as Mr. Zecevic said earlier, he never showed the extra documents, the 70-odd to the witness in proofing. However, Your Honours, this -- I mean, I know we're now wasting time almost more than that. We suggest that Mr. Zecevic puts these in through a bar table motion if that's what he wants to do. We do object to this witness who can do no more, whatever than his position, than say I read through these files, if that's what he wants to assert, that he's read through every single file ever submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What's wrong with that, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what is wrong, Your Honours, is that you might decide against me, and that is not the standard which was adopted in the -- during the Office of the Prosecutor's case. And I think that's unfair to the Defence, because the Office of the Prosecutor was allowed to bring all the documents where the witnesses were not even remotely acquainted with and were commenting on reading these documents, and all these documents were admitted. And the question -- when we objected, the question was never as -- the decision was never to suggest to the Office of the Prosecutor to include these documents in a bar table motion and ask that they be admitted through the bar table motion. That is the only reason why I'm doing this through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the purpose of this, as I would understand it, is to establish that in 1992 documents, statements, and whatever were established and you'll find them in the files in 2006 and 2007, 2008, whatever; right? So, there, I go along with you. But what happened in those trials in 2006, 2007, and 2008, that's not of any interest for us, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. What I'm introducing these documents is for the sole purpose that it shows that the Serb perpetrators for war crimes have been found guilty and sentenced based on the documentation partially prepared by the -- in 1992 or submitted by the MUP in 1992 together with the criminal complaints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, that's what I don't understand. What is the relevance -- the relevance about the fact that they have been convicted in 2008? The problem -- if the documents exist, and you have documents to show, then the question is what happened in 1992, what should have happened, what did happen, and what did not happen. But not what happened with that in 2008. Not the fact that criminals were convicted in 2008 upon those documents. I don't see the relevance of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but, Your Honours -- Your Honour, with all due respect, the job of the police is to file the criminal report and to gather the evidence on the investigation, on-site investigation, and all other expert knowledge and statements, gather all that as soon as possible after the commission of the crime, and they file the criminal report. And that is where the role of the police ends. We cannot -- Your Honours, we cannot -- also as in this Tribunal, these crimes have been committed in 1992. They are put on trial in 2009. That is the very same thing. Even the criminal complaints have been made in 1992. That is precisely the same thing. And now what I'm trying to establish right now is not -- it wasn't a part of our Defence case until Friday when Ms. Korner articulated the position of the Office of the Prosecutor. I never commented these documents with the witness.
