I haven't commented these, but I wasn't under notice that this is a part of the Prosecutor's case because they have been changing it, as I said at the very beginning. And now when it becomes clear, when it becomes clear, I have to take the measures in order to contradict the claims by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, it's the other way around. We haven't changed our case. The Defence asserted in one of their applications to add documents to their 65 ter that this point, the point that Mr. Zecevic is saying that we dispute, namely that the convictions in 2007 or the trials in 2007 result directly from the evidence gathered in 1992. And our response to that in writing over a week ago, if Mr. Zecevic read our response, was you could not possibly say that. There is nothing to show in these documents, any of them, on what the convictions are based. And that is the only issue that I raised last Thursday. And Mr. Zecevic can, as I say, in order -- if he thinks it's relevant -- my only objection at the moment is to this witness being used effectively as a mechanism to get these documents in when he can say nothing that actually goes to their admissibility or not. And that's the only objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But are we right, then, to conclude that the core of the issue here is whether in 1992 criminal reports were made and filed by the MUP? Because if that is the crux of the matter, then my question would be to Ms. Korner --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We don't dispute that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- if that is disputed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And if it is not disputed, then we come back to: What is the issue, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the issue, Your Honours, is a very simple one, because the Office of the Prosecutor will say, as they continue saying incorrectly, suggesting, that the filing of the criminal reports without the attachment of the statements and all that is nothing but sham inquiries or window dressing. That is their position. And when I say -- and when we show the judgements which contain the documents attached to the criminal reports that were filed in 1992 and based on which the trial chambers now are getting the convictions of these peoples or these perpetrators, then I think it's very relevant. That is our point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Zecevic, if I might reiterate the point that Ms. Korner has made: Since we aren't going to be led into ourselves, as it were, trying the cases which have been conducted in the region since 1992 based on that evidence, but only -- we are only concerned with the fact that that material which was gathered in 1992 has been used subsequently, what is your objection to batching this material and putting it forward in a bar table motion? Because, again, to repeat what Ms. Korner has said: What is this witness on the stand going to do other than to say that this is what these documents are, or something that a witness doesn't need to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I fully appreciate and understand your position and I might say to a certain extent I do agree. However, during the Prosecutor's case, Your Honour, let me remind you, we had -- we had members of the police, we had prosecutors, we had the judges who were commenting on the documents which were being presented to them for the first time when they received them from the Office of the Prosecutor, namely in 2009 or so, and they commented on that, and all their testimony and all these documents were admitted by the Trial Chamber. That is precisely the same situation as here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Zecevic, if your analysis of what the Chamber did then is accurate, why would you be inviting us to repeat what, in your view, is an error? Shouldn't we correct it at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying Your Honour committed an error. Not at all, with all due respect. What I'm saying is that this is a different standard which is applied during the Defence case. That is my only problem which I'm having. That there is a different standard now when we are presenting our Defence case to the standard that we had adopted during the Prosecutor's case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We simply don't agree. Your Honours made exactly the same points to us, that we couldn't use witnesses simply to get documents in and we had to bar table them, and that's what we did. So we suggest that's the right way of doing it. And can we get on and get this witness to deal with something he actually knows something about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's time for the break. We will deal with this when we come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, to the extent that the Chamber understands what -- the importance of these documents on which you wish to rely, our recollection is that faced with a similar problem, when the Prosecution was conducting its case, it was suggested that the course -- the most practical course was to lead oral evidence from the witness on the stand to present and lay down a sampling of the type of documents and then the bulk was brought in by way of a separate motion. So that is what we are thinking could or should be done in this case, that -- and in that vein, may I inquire as to how -- what is your bulk like? We've seen one or two samples. How many documents are we talking about altogether?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have altogether six documents, Your Honours, six judgements, which we requested in our motion that five of them be admitted on the 65 ter list. And this is a pending motion. And one document is on our 65 ter list and I would ask that this one be admitted and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, to save time, we will not object to the admission on to the 65 ter list nor into evidence of these documents, those six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's move quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, should I read on the record the numbers of documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, since you have them, yes, that would save more time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So first document is 906D1. It's tab --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, as a -- perhaps I'm being - what's the word? - pernickety, but don't we have to have the witness on the stand and formally admit the sample and then go for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I'm sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honours, I'm not sure that we do. I think we can. As we are not disputing it, they can just read them out and Your Honours admit them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. I was just -- I just thought that the list had to be admitted against an exhibit, but we haven't yet exhibited anything. That was the only point I was making. So this one would be exhibited, but the witness -- does the witness have to be on the stand for it to be tendered, that's the only ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So this is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. 906D1 is the first document. Shall we admit that one first? And then the rest.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D596, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, the next document is 905D1, tab 284. And the following document is 907D1, tab 286. Then 908D1, tab 287. Then 909D1, tab 288. And 910D1, tab 289. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, exhibit numbers assigned will be 1D597 through 1D601.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, awhile ago we saw the destiny of criminal reports filed for crimes perpetrated by members of the Serbian people in 1992. What was the destiny of the criminal reports filed in 1992 encompassing crimes committed by the other ethnic groups with the Serbs as victims?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regrettably, nothing was done about those criminal reports. I could explain, if you like. All the criminal reports filed by the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska and dually submitted to the relevant prosecutors based on our information, and our information was reliable, first of all seemed to be passed along from one prosecutor to the next one down the line. The military prosecutor would forward a case to a civilian prosecutor, and a civilian prosecutor would send the case file back to the military prosecutor. From there it went on to the district prosecutor. And then depending on the changing regulations, something else would happen next. This Tribunal probably knows about the fact that so-called rules of the Roman path were adopted. The criminal files or formal reports in this case ended up here in The Hague. When the prosecutor's office in Bosnia-Herzegovina was established, the BH courts, the reports were delivered to the BH prosecutor's office. To this very day, over 90 per cent of those cases are still at the investigation stage. The same stage, in other words, that these cases were at back in 1992 or indeed back in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Zecevic, that page 56 line 2 should read "rules of the road," as opposed to "rules of the Roman path" which is a great description.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tusevljak, I only have a couple of questions left for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the witness 65 ter 20187, OTP tab 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You don't have it in that binder. The document was announced later on, and you will see it's come up on the monitor, on the screen in front of you. Mr. Tusevljak, your own service for investigating war crimes was also assisting whenever a defence request arose to deliver documents, was that not the case?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever we received a request, quite regardless of whether the request in question was from the OTP or from the Defence, we would grant access to all of the documents available to us, in keeping with the laws and regulations. Needless to say, each time we would clearly stress that the documents could only be used for the purposes of a trial and that these documents were by no means to be published or indeed used for any other purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the date on this document is the 15th of November, 2007, signed by team co-ordinator Simo Tusevljak. Is this one of your documents, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, among other things, at page 4 of the Serbian and number 50, could you please comment specifically on what the documentation that you delivered to the Stanisic Defence is in relation to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5 of the English. Number 50.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure specifically what this is about. There are just too many documents. The documents were prepared by my units, my service, not me personally. Which means, when I look at this, it's obvious that this was about an expert opinion, obtaining an expert opinion on something. But it's impossible for me to address each document separately and tell you what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you just look at the documents which are in your binder under tabs 210 through to 256. Just glance through them, please, and tell us whether you are familiar with these documents.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are documents that are available to us. At the moment, in our archives, we have thousands, perhaps even hundreds of thousands, of various documents which are all stacked in cupboards and which specifically have to do with war crimes. Not just where the seat of my team is located in Pale, but also in departments located in the territory of Republika Srpska that I co-ordinate. That includes Banja Luka, Doboj, Bijeljina, Trebinje, and Sarajevo, which has a separate department.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, all these documents which I asked you to glance at are some sorts of expert opinions. Please tell me whether these documents have been submitted to the Prosecutor's Office of this Tribunal. Or let me ask a more specific question: The documents which have been seized from the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka, have they been submitted to the Prosecutor's office of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something I couldn't know. But if The Hague investigators seized these documents, then they should have submitted all these documents to the Prosecutor's Office. Why would they have seized it otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in 1998 the complete documentation of the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka was seized by ICTY Prosecutor's Office investigators?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, sorry, I'm perfectly prepared to concede, we've said this a number of times, that a large quantity of documents were seized from the CSB. I'm not prepared to say that the complete was seized because I'm aware that some rooms weren't searched and that's why we've been finding a loft financial information. None of the financial information, for example, was taken at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please tell me, as you have glanced at the documents which I pointed out to you under these tabs 210 through to 250, were these the documents which were submitted to us under item 50 in 2007?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it should be that that's it, because these are the -- this is the expertise of different traces found at the scene by the crime technicians during 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, considering the position of the Trial Chamber stated on page 7840, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The letter? No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, document or documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document, Your Honour, the letter from the RS which is 65 ter 20187, tab 52. I believe it's in front of Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D602, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry. Tab 52?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Our bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That one, it has a P number, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] On your list it has.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Delvoie, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It hasn't. Okay. It's on your list with a P number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. And based on this, Your Honours, and in light of the decision of the Trial Chamber handed down, oral decision, on page 7840 during the testimony of Tutus, Vladimir, I would move the Trial Chamber at this point to de-MFI the documents 1D214 until 1D232. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it went a bit further than that, when there was an attempt not, in fact, to put in all the documents that Mr. Zecevic referred to, but only the ones that were MFI, whereas I think Mr. Zecevic is now trying to put in every single solitary one under each tab; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm just talking about the documents which were mentioned during the testimony of Mr. Tutus on page 7840 and further, and it contains the numbers 1D214 until number 1D232. And all the documents were MFI'd, and they were MFI'd because of the proof of authenticity -- pending matter of authenticity being resolved at some point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, it's a bit more complicated than that. But, Your Honours, can I ask this: I do have some questions about this letter and these documents, and may I ask that you wait before making a decision, and also give me a chance to recheck this, until the end of cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's fine with me, Your Honours. Your Honours, thank you, I have no further questions for this witness. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no questions for this witness. Otherwise, if we started, we would have to deal with around 7.000 criminal reports which Mr. Stojan Zupljanin filed, so we won't be asking the witness anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Noted. Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know how proper that is, but still.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, you told the Court at page 22193 that you enrolled in this police academy in Skopje in 1984 and were there for four years, until 1988; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you went to the SJB in Novi Grad in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That was your first job in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And unlike we've heard from some witnesses, during the course of your four-year study, you didn't actually take time out, did you, to go and work as a member of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just had practical work after the second and third years of study. It was a month on each occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So by the time the conflict broke out and the split took place in the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you had actually only been working for around three years as a police officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly three years.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So it be right to say, wouldn't it, that you weren't, perhaps, the most experienced of police officers?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certain if I only had three years of work experience behind me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And whilst you were at Novi Grad, you were an inspector in the -- an ordinary inspector in the SUP -- oh, sorry, in the police station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the crime police department.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you moved to the SUP in Sarajevo, and originally, when you first joined the RS MUP, is that right - just let me find the right page - you worked out of -- sorry, you did tell us which police station it was. Oh, it was the police station at your home address -- at your home in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the 4th of April, 1992, that was the reserve police station. It was not the typical police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And did you then move to the CSB Sarajevo, you told us, in early June 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I was in the crime police administration, and that was where I was registered in the month of May. I'm not certain but for a while I was an inspector at the crime police station administration at the level of the Republika Srpska MUP. That means not at the Security Services Centre but, rather, at the administration, but it was just for a short period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Fine. So during the course of that time when you were still an inspector, did you have dealings with prisoners of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: None at all?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us later on, I think on Friday, quite a lot about what's commonly called Kula Prison but I think is properly called the Butmir Prison facility; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We call it the Kula Prison. And I live nearby. I'm living close to that prison even today. So when it comes to that prison, this is something I'm familiar with even though I didn't work in the police. My house is perhaps 200 metres away from that prison, and I pass by it practically every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. As I say, you gave a very detailed description of the SJB and the prison as they were in 1992, so do we take it from that that you visited those premises on a number of occasions?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prison is the same today as it was back then. The administrative building is in the same place and so is the detention unit. And we then took the measures of detention for persons who had committed criminal offences. That was not just in 1992, but to the end of the war there was a detention unit there. A detention unit where we would send someone to be detained for 72 hours, that if we took such a measure, this was a place where such persons were sent to be detained there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But at the time it also had the SJB, didn't it, in the same premises, divided, as you told us, by a wall?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the very beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you were shown by Mr. Zecevic a document which is at your tab 205, and I think its number is 1D591. And you told us that this document was never submitted to the -- sorry, you said you'd never seen this document and you don't know why it says that. Is that correct? That's at page 22376.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I haven't seen this document. The first time it was when it was shown to me by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But wasn't it right that the SJB at Kula was actually keeping Muslim prisoners at the SJB?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the Kula Police Station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I used to enter the administrative building. I would drop by, because while it was still possible to go across the Sarajevo airport from Nedzarici, to go there and back, when I went to the school at Vrace, this is what I was talking about, I wanted to see what my assignment was and where I would be deployed. We would drop by to this police station to ask whether we could go across the Sarajevo airport, because at the time it was under enemy fire. You would walk along the runway because the airport was not open as such. No planes landed or took off, but you could cross the runway of the airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about that for the moment. This document is dated the 13th of June and the airport was taken over by UNPROFOR at the beginning of June, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, around the beginning of June this possibility of crossing over ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So I'm asking you how you know that prisoners were not being kept at the SJB Kula instead of the prison facilities.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you that, first of all, I had not seen this document and another thing is that I did not see prisoners in the administration building. This is the basis on which I'm telling you this. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you, from your knowledge, can think of no reason why Mr. Mandic instead of sending this to the prison should be sending this to the Kula SJB?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not because the Ministry of Justice and the MUP have nothing in common. They are two separate organisational units, completely separate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I've just got to trace because we altered the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, just for the clarity of the transcript, if Ms. Korner would be so kind to clarify the existence of the SJB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought that was what he said. And we've got documents showing it exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can take his phones off -- headphones off.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you could please take your headphones off, Mr. Tusevljak. [In English] The point of the matter is that the witness's testimony during the direct was that it exist -- there existed no such thing as SJB Kula. Well, I will find the reference in the transcript. What he testified about was that the SJB Novo Sarajevo, New Sarajevo, was at the administrative building in front of the Butmir KPD, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And your question was directed at the SJB Kula, so -- and he confirmed that no such thing existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, he seemed to understand what I was talking about. Whether it's technically called the SJB Kula or not - and we'll be dealing with that with documents - as my understanding is, there was no argument there was a police station, even if it was part of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is no argument that the SJB Novo Sarajevo was stationed at the administrative building in front of the Butmir KPD prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Could we have document -- Your Honours, I'm so sorry. Because of the additions we've made to the list, I've completely confused myself as to where my document is. Yes. Could we look, please, at Exhibit P1633, which is behind tab 3 in the Prosecution bundle, so Mr. Tusevljak won't have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tusevljak, are you familiar with this book? It's the duty book held by the Kula KP.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look, please, at the second --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to the second page in English, and it's the third page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to look at the last entry. Does that read: "On the 2nd of May, 1992, criminal inspectors Dejan Vaskovic and Simo Tusevljak took from the police station Kula" I think that is the SM Kula, whatever its correct name have been - is that Stanica Milicije or something like that? - "to Pale the following persons:" And it lists those people. Is that you? And, sorry, in B/C/S you'd have to look at the next page as well to see the list of people.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I thought you told us not five minutes ago that you had no dealings with Muslim prisoners while you were an inspector.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't think these are Muslim prisoners but perpetrators of criminal offences, and I think this had to do with drugs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. First of all, you make a distinction, do you, when I say people -- "prisoners," you make a distinction between that and a perpetrator of a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about the difference because we detained, I mean the crime police, detained persons who were suspected of having perpetrated a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Were these people, or at least some of them, of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were, four of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And you're saying, are you, that on the 2nd of May you were dealing with drug offences when the conflict had just broken out?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if someone from the police took in these people because perhaps they searched them at the check-point and found drugs, this was probably why we took them over. Or maybe it was something else that was not in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And is the SM Kula, described here, the same police station that we've been -- that you were talking about earlier and I was asking you about earlier, based in the Kula Prison, or within the compound of the Kula Prison?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the administration building, rather than within the compound of the prison. In the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And whether properly or not, whether this was supposed to be part of Novo Sarajevo, it was call the Kula SJB, wasn't it, or SM?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had various names. It was supposed to be the Public Security Station Novi Grad, but it says here Kula.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's what everybody called it, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly because of the location where it was, that was how it was called. Now, whether it was officially an SM or an SJB, that's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And why were you taking them to Pale, may I ask?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably for the investigation to continue over there of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then why Pale? You weren't working at Pale.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by the 2nd of May we didn't have a Security Services Centre really. Nor, indeed, were we unable to put in any quality police work. Nor, indeed, did we have a proper prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've said that, and I'll come back to all of that now, but I want to know why you as an inspector from the station that you were in May were taking people from Kula to Pale?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As for this other well-known criminal, I don't even really remember this, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, which other well-known criminal?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nihad Rovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it couldn't have been, could it, for the purposes of some kind of prisoner exchange, rather like the letter we saw from Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not so involved in any of these exchanges at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to, as it were, deal with your career. When did you acquire your present position?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My present position, in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you've been supplying documents to the Stanisic Defence since at least 2007 and have you been co-operating with them since before that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know. It was the moment we started receiving formal requests.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you have meetings with Mr. Stanisic personally?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, once.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just once?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically. Perhaps 2007 and perhaps not. I really don't know. The indictment had been published already and then he was provisionally released at one time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did he come to see you or did you go and see him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had some contacts in Belgrade with the war crimes prosecutor. We were working on some things together and I was working with Serbia's MUP again. I think it was at one of those meetings that I met Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Apart from what you've been asked to corroborate in this letter for the purposes of documents for court, have you provided other documents to Mr. Stanisic and/or Mr. Stanisic's lawyers?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just what is included in the file.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just one clarification. I don't believe the witness's answer, the previous answer, was correctly recorded. 70/3 and 4. "I think it was at one of those meetings that I met Mr. Stanisic." And he was talking about some MUP meetings and war crime prosecutor, and I think the witness said something different. Can you please, for the sake of clarity, clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll repeat the question I asked you. When you met Mr. Stanisic, you say on that one occasion, where did you meet him and how -- well, first of all, where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade. I don't know Belgrade well. It was in a restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you meet him? Did he ask to meet you? Did you ask to meet him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I never thought about it then or afterwards. I think it was by accident. Perhaps Stanisic found out from someone that I was around, so he gave me a call. I think that's how it was, but I didn't think about it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You are being asked to repeat the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't thinking about it, the reason I met this person who was, in fact, my minister, my superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, but at that stage you say you knew he'd been indicted by this Tribunal and he was no longer your minister or your superior. Were you friendly with him during 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly. I met Mr. Stanisic when he came from Cetar [phoen], the Sarajevo SUP, when he became the secretary of Sarajevo's SUP. During that time I met him maybe two or three times. Afterwards, we got to know each other a little better when he became minister of the interior of Republika Srpska. And Mr. Stanisic was there twice. I got to know him better the second time around when he became minister of the interior, because at the time I worked with the crime police administration in Bijeljina and I was in charge of certain activities, uncovering some serious crimes. And that was when we got to know each other better and became closer friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And just a final one question before I move on to another topic: How did he have your telephone number?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My telephone number is public. One of my friends probably passed it on to him. My telephone number is easy enough to find in a directory, perhaps in one of my business cards which I distributed thousands and thousands of. It really wasn't a problem for anyone who wished to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to come on to this centre for war crimes investigations which you head. It's right, isn't it, that you don't have in your archives one single original document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that we don't have a single original document. What the Republika Srpska MUP did in relation to our own activities from 2005 on, it's all originals. The greatest problem for us was when we started this activity in 2005 was precisely this. We were unable to retrieve the original documentation. First we got from you a total of 23 or 24 DVDs, copied documents, documentation that the OTP investigators seized from the Republika Srpska MUP or the public security stations throughout the territory. We also asked the people from the war crimes investigation centre in Belgrade and they accommodated us. We spent a full three months making copies of their documents. We were also given some documents from our own war crimes investigation centre in Banja Luka, which is part of the justice ministry. We also contacted all the NGOs who we had learned were in possession in some documents -- in possession of some documents related to war crimes, so we tried to obtain those too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not -- can I put it this way, Mr. Tusevljak: I'm not criticizing you. I'm merely asking for a fact. The reality is, and for the reasons you described, you don't have a single original document prior to, as you say, 2005? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 90 per cent of the cases, the documents were like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And, again, please, I'm not criticizing you for this at all, but you have absolutely no method whatsoever of assessing whether your documents that you have got from various sources, I accept, are authentic or not authentic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we do. When we enclose a document like that and send it to the prosecutor, normally we get a request from the prosecutor. And this was very often the case. We go back to whoever we got the document from in order to obtain a certified copy of the document. It was the case on several occasions that documents obtained from the war crimes investigation centre in Belgrade would be forwarded to the BH prosecutor and then the BH prosecutor would seek international legal assistance and would ask that the court in Belgrade confirm the authenticity of whatever document, which they would invariably do. Likewise, if we knew that the documents were from The Hague Tribunal, we would advise the prosecutor to again seek co-operation and get the original documents from the OTP or from the Tribunal itself. Therefore, that was the only way to prove the authenticity of the documents we were using in our own court proceedings. We were not able to examine or cross-examine those who produced those documents, unlike you. That, you will agree, is a job for the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For any of that list of documents that was on that letter Mr. Zecevic showed you, did you go back to the originators and say, Can you certify that these are genuine, proper, that the originals are genuine documents produced on the date and at the time that it appears to say?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in some of the letters and exchanges we would even clearly point out that the documents in question were copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, I mean, I'm simply asking you about that letter. And you can take it with you, if you like, a copy of it. And whether, in respect of any of the documents, the 170 I think it is, you are able to say that you got a certificate to say these are the originals properly produced at the time and by the people who they appear to be?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one asked us to do that. We're simply asked whether we had documents available in our archives and whether we had the copies too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you also told the Trial Chamber about your work with, you say, the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could you tell the Court, please - and if may be better, I suppose, if we go into private session for this - the names of the investigations on which you have worked for the -- or with the prosecutor's office of BiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think we need to have the blinds for private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you, please, Mr. Tusevljak, to take with you tonight a copy of the CSB Sarajevo KU book, and I would like you, please, to go through it and check to see whether you have any criminal reports in this going up until 1995, which I think it runs up to, for Serbs committing crimes against non-Serbs, war crimes. Whether they're described as murders, you've told us, or war crimes. And secondly, I'm going to give you, because there was a complaint last time about this, a copy of the MUP report, that came out in January of 1993, the annual report, which doesn't appear that Mr. Zecevic showed you, so that you can take that away and read that overnight. Unless there's an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, has this document ever been disclosed to the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It has. I don't know when. All the Prosecutor's log-books were disclosed. KU books.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It has the number 20188.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That doesn't mean -- we haven't used it. But it was disclosed. All the Prosecutor's books -- all the KU books have been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please provide us with a date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I will. Tomorrow. I'd like him to have it back, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I will have the objection if it's not disclosed before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want him to have it. Would Your Honours allow the usher to give him that document and this one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Batch 110, 5th of March, 2010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, Mr. Tusevljak, do you understand what it is the Prosecution is requesting of you? Do you have any questions that you would want to put to her through the Chamber before we rise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is just one of the logs that we kept for reports submitted directly by the Security Services Centre. Public security stations in the centre area had their own registers, and the total number of criminal reports filed would be added up based on those received by the police stations and this register. But, yes, I do understand what Ms. Korner is expecting me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we take the adjournment to tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 21st day of June, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
